summary: This informational RFC makes specifications of cryptographic algorithms based on the Russian national standards GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 available to the Internet community. They cover pseudorandom functions, key agreement based on Diffie-Hellman, and a hash function for use in cryptographic protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7836 specifies supporting algorithms for cryptographic protocols that use GOST 2012 standards. It describes how to authenticate data, agree on keys, derive keys, and wrap keys, with examples for testing implementations.

subtitle: Algorithm specifications for protocols using the GOST 2012 signature and hash standards.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic protocols need interoperable specifications for algorithms that accompany the GOST R 34.10-2012 signature standard and GOST R 34.11-2012 hash standard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes HMAC and pseudorandom functions, VKO key agreement, key-derivation functions, key wrapping, and elliptic-curve parameter sets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7836 is an Informational Independent Submission providing algorithm details and test examples. The RFC Editor makes no statement about the document's value for implementation or deployment.

today: RFC 7836 is an Informational RFC published in the Independent Submission stream. The RFC Editor states that publication does not express a view about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: Supporting Algorithms for GOST Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 7836 describes algorithms based on Russian standards GOST R 34.10-2012 for digital signatures and GOST R 34.11-2012 for hashing. It provides specifications intended to help implement cryptographic protocols using those standards.

The RFC defines terminology and byte-order conventions used by its algorithms. Its scope includes HMAC functions, pseudorandom functions, key agreement, elliptic-curve parameters, key derivation, and key export functions.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC provides detailed recipes for cryptographic tools that use GOST 2012 standards. It defines conventions so implementations can process the same inputs and outputs consistently.

sections.title: HMAC and Pseudorandom Functions
sections.content:
The RFC specifies HMAC transformations built on the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function. The 256-bit variant produces 32 bytes of output, and the 512-bit variant produces 64 bytes.

It also defines HMAC-based pseudorandom functions for TLS and IKEv2 use. The TLS variants combine a protocol-assigned label and seed with a secret; the IKEv2 variants use the specified HMAC functions within its PRF+ processing. Protocols assign the label and seed values, and the RFC says their lengths should be fixed by the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: HMAC uses a secret key and a hash function to produce an authentication value. The RFC defines two output sizes and pseudorandom functions that protocols can use with them.

sections.title: Key Agreement and Derivation
sections.content:
The two VKO algorithms let parties agree on keying material using elliptic-curve keys and a User Keying Material (UKM) value. VKO_GOSTR3410_2012_256 produces 256-bit keying material and supports public keys of at least 512 bits. VKO_GOSTR3410_2012_512 produces 512-bit keying material and requires public keys of at least 1024 bits.

The tree KDF uses HMAC_GOSTR3411_2012_256 repeatedly to generate keying material at a requested size, and its outputs can be used to form a hierarchy of derived keys. The simpler KDF_GOSTR3411_2012_256 is the tree function with specified parameters that produce a 256-bit result.
sections.plainLanguage: VKO lets two parties calculate matching secret key material from their private and public keys. The key-derivation functions then produce keys for a protocol, including a hierarchy of keys when needed.

sections.title: Wrapping Keys for Transfer or Storage
sections.content:
The key-wrap process protects a secret key using an export key and GOST 28147-89. It generates a random seed, derives an encryption key with KDF_GOSTR3411_2012_256, calculates a four-byte message authentication code over the key, and encrypts the key in Electronic Codebook mode.

The wrapped representation contains the seed, encrypted key, and MAC. To unwrap it, the recipient derives the same encryption key, decrypts the key, calculates the MAC again, and reports an error if the calculated value does not match the transmitted MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: Key wrapping encrypts a key and includes a check value to detect changes. Unwrapping recreates the encryption key, decrypts the data, and verifies the check value.

sections.title: Curve Parameters and Security
sections.content:
The RFC recommends elliptic-curve parameters and object identifiers for use with the GOST signature and key-agreement algorithms. It defines 512-bit prime-modulus curves in canonical form and also describes twisted Edwards representations; for 256-bit canonical curves, it points to parameters in RFC 4357. The RFC does not prohibit other curve parameters.

The Security Considerations section states that the entire document concerns security considerations. The specifications include example values and test cases for checking algorithm implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC supplies recommended curve parameters and identifiers so implementations can agree on the same curves. It also includes test examples and says its subject throughout is security.
